t: Find the Sum of Subsequence Powers
o: Sum, over all size-k subsequences, the minimum pairwise absolute difference. After sorting a subsequence, that minimum is always achieved by two consecutive sorted elements. Sort nums globally; for a pair (i, j), i < j, with gap g = nums[j] − nums[i] to be the leftmost minimum-gap pair of a subsequence: no chosen element lies strictly between i and j (any such element would create a smaller gap), all chosen elements left of i must be MORE than g below nums[i] (otherwise an equally-small pair with a smaller left endpoint exists), and elements right of j must be at least g above nums[j]. The count is then C(|L| + |R|, k − 2), where L and R are the eligible pools. Verified on the examples: [1,2,3,4], k=3 gives 2+1+1 = 4; [4,3,−1], k=2 gives 4+5+1 = 10.
k: Sort; the power of a subsequence equals the minimum gap between consecutive sorted chosen values.
Charge each subsequence to its unique leftmost minimum-gap pair (i, j): nothing chosen strictly between them, left pool strictly farther than g, right pool at least g away.
Contribution of pair (i, j) is g · C(|L| + |R|, k − 2), found with binary search.

a.n: Approach 1: Pair charging with binomial coefficients
a.i: Enumerate all O(n²) pairs of the sorted array as the charged minimum pair. Eligible left indices are those with nums[idx] < nums[i] − g (found by lower_bound); eligible right indices satisfy nums[idx] ≥ nums[j] + g. Any k − 2 picks from the combined pool complete a valid subsequence, counted by a binomial coefficient.
s: Sort nums and precompute Pascal's triangle up to n.
For each pair i < j compute g, L = count of indices with value < nums[i] − g, R = count with value ≥ nums[j] + g.
Add g · C(L + R, k − 2) to the answer modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n² log n) — n² pairs each with two binary searches; binomials precomputed.

a.i: Enumerate every size-k combination of the sorted array and add its minimum consecutive gap. Exponential, but a perfect correctness oracle for stress-testing the combinatorial solution on tiny inputs.
s: Recursively build all size-k index combinations in order.
For each completed combination add the minimum consecutive difference.
a.t: O(C(n, k) · k) — exponential; only for validation.

w: The pair-charging argument is the heart: prove uniqueness of the leftmost minimum pair (ties on the right are fine, ties on the left are forbidden by the strict inequality). Pitfalls: forgetting to sort, mixing up strict vs non-strict bounds on the two sides, and 64-bit gaps (values up to 1e8 in magnitude give gaps up to 2e8 — reduce mod before multiplying). Follow-up: sum of SECOND-smallest gaps, or k-subsequence powers under a different metric like max−min.
